newsitem.title: UK: Chemicals give migraines that throbbing pain.
newsitem.headline: Chemicals give migraines that throbbing pain.

text.p: Chemicals that cause inflammation may be responsible for the throbbing pain of a migraine headache, U.S. scientists reported on Wednesday.
Experiments on rats show nerves and blood vessels associated with the meninges or membranes between the brain and skull are highly sensitive to naturally occurring chemicals in the body.

Andrew Strassman of the Harvard medical school and colleagues noted that although no one really knows what causes a migraine, such headaches have a lot in common with the pain that accompanies a brain tumour or haemmorhage or meningitis -- an inflammation of the meninges.
Such headaches worsen with movement such as shaking.
Blood vessels are believed to be involved, but Strassman's group decided to test whether inflammatory chemicals such as histamines might be a factor.
They cut open the skulls of rats, exposing the nerves in the meninges.
They irritated these nerves with salt solution, capsaicin, which gives hot peppers their bite, and "a soup of inflammatory agents" such as histamine, the hormone serotonin and a prostaglandin.
The nerves reacted strongly, which would probably translate to severe pain such as that seen in a headache.

They said inflammation of the meninges seemed to come from the release of chemicals known as neuropeptides from the connections between the brain and the membranes, which in turn causes the release of inflammatory chemicals like histamines.
This could be one of the mysterious forces behind the throbbing pain of a migraine, they wrote in a report in the science journal Nature.
